title: Act II, Scene I

teacherSummary.text: After the feast Romeo hides in the Capulet orchard. Mercutio and Benvolio call for him; Mercutio mockingly conjures him by Rosaline's body parts. Benvolio says love is blind; they go home.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act II, Scene I,” how does Shakespeare show Mercutio's mockery outside the orchard? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act II, Scene I, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of Mercutio's mockery outside the orchard? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act II, Scene I develops the idea of Mercutio's mockery outside the orchard. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act II, Scene I (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of Mercutio's mockery outside the orchard. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act II, Scene I suggests about Mercutio's mockery outside the orchard. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's characterization and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses characterization in Act II, Scene I to complicate the reader's understanding of Mercutio's mockery outside the orchard. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act II, Scene I within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Mercutio's mockery outside the orchard responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act II, Scene I alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Mercutio's mockery outside the orchard follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act II, Scene I and its treatment of Mercutio's mockery outside the orchard. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act II, Scene I as evidence for a larger claim about Mercutio's mockery outside the orchard in Romeo and Juliet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act II, Scene I as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Mercutio's mockery outside the orchard. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Romeo and Juliet.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: light and dark
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: The lovers describe each other as light in darkness (torches, sun, stars, lightning), yet they can meet only at night, and daylight brings danger. In this scene: “himself among these trees, / To be consorted with the humorous night: / Blind is his love and best befits the dark” (Act II, Scene I, Benvolio (speech 8)).

symbolsAndMotifs.name: names and identity
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Names carry the feud ("Montague," "Capulet"); Juliet wishes a name were only a word. In this scene: “my invocation / Is fair and honest, and in his mistress’ name / I conjure only but to raise up him” (Act II, Scene I, Mercutio (speech 7)).

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
